mem.t: Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility and subject yourselves to one another; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

lessons.title: The Many Faces of Pride
lessons.theme: Pride wears a thousand disguises, but it has one root: self-centredness

v: Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.
For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit, like a doctor holding a magnifying glass, to examine your heart gently: “Lord, show me the pride in me that is hard to detect.” Wait quietly. Don't rush to defend yourself; just note the first picture that comes to mind.
teach: What makes a virus so hard to guard against is that it mutates: it changes its outward form while its nature stays the same. Pride is like that. In the first stage we learned that pride is leaving our place and grasping power. Last week we asked to be filled with the Spirit, and pride is the number one obstacle to the Spirit. Today we learn to recognise pride's many variants, because the most dangerous pride is often the kind we fail to recognise.

Paul asked the self-important Corinthians three questions: Who makes you different? What do you have that you didn't receive? And if you received it, why do you boast? These three questions demolish every foundation of pride — everything we have, we have received. Proverbs warns: pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.

Pride has obvious faces: boasting, looking down on others, refusing to be taught, needing to control. It also has hidden faces: self-pity (“Nobody understands me”), excessive self-blame (“How could I have failed?”), people-pleasing (caring too much about our image), and spiritual superiority. They all have one root: being centred on self. Eyes held high and eyes cast down may both be looking only at ourselves.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our place and grasping power — wanting to be our own god, and other people's god too. Pride is the outward expression of the self-ruled life; only by recognising its many disguises can we treat it properly. Humility is the key to revival, and that key begins with honestly seeing ourselves.
q: Who is God? — “What do you have that you didn't receive?” What does this show you about God as the Giver?
Who am I? — Which face of pride shows up most often in you: boasting, controlling, self-pity, or people-pleasing?
How shall I respond? — When that face appears today, how will you recognise it and hand it to the Lord?
lessons.jesus: On earth, Jesus spoke of everything as received: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7:16). He possessed everything yet took no credit; we have nothing of our own, yet often want the credit. He is the perfect pattern of the self-emptied life.
lessons.pray: Lord, search me and show me the disguised pride in my heart: boasting, controlling, self-pity, people-pleasing. I confess that everything I have, I have received from you, and I have nothing to boast about. Tear down my self-centredness and bring me back to my place. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down the face of pride that shows up most often in you, and what triggers it
Today, change one “I did it” into “Thank you, Lord, for enabling me to do it”
Ask a trusted companion to tell you one blind spot they see in you
lessons.noon: “And what do you have that you didn’t receive?” — Lord, right now I acknowledge that everything comes from you.

lessons.title: Two Men Who Prayed
lessons.theme: God looks not at the length of a prayer but at the heart of the one praying

v: “Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed by himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men: extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.’
But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

lessons.still: Be still for a moment in the posture of the tax collector: bow your head, with no need to find any reason to score points for yourself. Come before God with a single sentence: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” Repeat it slowly, and let your heart catch up with your lips.
teach: Two men stood in the same temple doing the same thing — praying — yet the outcomes were worlds apart. Jesus told this parable “to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others” (18:9). The sharpest point of the parable is this: after reading it, it is very easy to think, “Thank God I'm not like that Pharisee” — and in that moment we have become the Pharisee.

The Pharisee “prayed to himself” — on the surface he was speaking to God, but really he was talking to himself. Every line of his prayer revolves around “I,” focused entirely on his own performance and other people's failures. The tax collector stood “far away” and “beat his breast,” asking only for mercy. The word “be merciful” is linked to the Old Testament mercy seat and atonement: he was asking for God's covering, not God's approval.

Religious pride is the hardest to cure, because it wears spiritual clothing. If our Bible reading, prayer and giving become capital for comparing ourselves with others, they turn from channels of grace into stepping stones of pride. Here is the change of mindset: the purpose of spiritual disciplines is not to make me better than others, but to make me more dependent on God and closer to him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Pharisee's focus was on himself and on others; the tax collector's focus was on God. “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted” is the spiritual law of humility. Let God be God: only he can justify, so I don't need to justify myself.
q: Who is God? — What does the God who justified the tax collector value in a person?
Who am I? — Have your spiritual disciplines ever quietly become capital for comparing yourself with others?
How shall I respond? — Which posture of the tax collector will you take as you come before God today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners and was criticised for it (Luke 15:1–2). He said, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke 5:32). In his presence, those who admit their need are the first to receive grace.
lessons.pray: God, be merciful to me, a sinner! I lay down my spiritual résumé and stop using others' failures to make myself look good. I confess that I need your covering and your mercy. Do not let my Bible reading and prayer become stepping stones of pride, but a deeper dependence on you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: When you pray today, don't mention what you have done; simply ask the Lord for mercy
When you catch yourself comparing with someone in your heart, immediately bless that person
Notice how many times the word “I” appears in your prayers
lessons.noon: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” — Lord, right now I look only to your mercy.

lessons.title: Nebuchadnezzar Humbled
lessons.theme: God can humble the proud, and he can restore the humble

v: The king spoke and said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?”
Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase.

lessons.still: Lift your eyes to heaven, as Nebuchadnezzar did when he was restored. Say to the Lord, “You are the King of heaven; I am your creature.” Quietly place the achievement you are proudest of back into the Lord's hands.
teach: A great tree grows until it reaches the sky and begins to think it is holding the sky up. That is exactly the tree Nebuchadnezzar saw in his dream — cut down, with only the stump left (Daniel 4). A year later, walking on the roof of his palace, he boasted, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built…?” — and while the words were still in his mouth, judgement fell.

This chapter traces a turning line through the word “I.” In verse 30: “the might of my power,” “the glory of my majesty” — all the credit goes to himself. In verse 34: “I lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me” — his turning begins with looking up. In verse 37: “I… praise and extol and honor the King of heaven” — the same “I,” but now focused on God. Pride made him like a beast; humility restored him to being human.

God humbles the proud not to destroy them but to restore them: leaving the stump means leaving hope. Sometimes God allows us to lose health, position or plans so that we may know that “the Most High rules in the kingdom of men” (4:25). Here is the change of mindset: when you are humbled, don't only ask “Why?” — ask even more, “Lord, what place do you want me to return to?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our human place and wanting to be God — and ending up unable even to be human. Humility is returning to our place: letting people be people and letting God be God. In the end Nebuchadnezzar gave all praise, honour and glory to the King of heaven — this is letting God receive all the glory.
q: Who is God? — “The Most High rules in the kingdom of men.” What does this mean for your situation today?
Who am I? — Is there a “great Babylon” in your life that you secretly believe you built yourself?
How shall I respond? — How will you “lift your eyes to heaven” today and give the glory to God?
lessons.jesus: Nebuchadnezzar tried to rise from man to god and sank to the level of a beast; Jesus, existing in the form of God, humbled himself to become man, and God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:9). The way of pride is grasping upward and falling; the way of humility is stooping downward and being lifted up.
lessons.pray: King of heaven, you rule in the kingdom of men. I confess that I have taken the achievements you gave me as my own credit. I lift my eyes to heaven and give all praise, honour and glory to you. If you need to humble me, please also restore me, and bring me back to my place as a human being. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Pick one of your achievements and write down every part of it that you “received”
When someone praises you, name specifically the help you had from God or from others
Read Daniel 4 and notice God's patience and his warnings
lessons.noon: “And those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” — Lord, right now I humble myself before you.

lessons.title: Clothed with Humility
lessons.theme: Humility is not a passing posture but clothing we put on every day

v: Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility and subject yourselves to one another; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time,
casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

lessons.still: Picture yourself getting dressed in the morning and, last of all, tying on an apron. Say to the Lord, “Lord, today I clothe myself with humility.” Then take one thing that is worrying you and, like slipping off a heavy backpack, cast it onto him.
teach: In ancient times, servants tied a cloth around their waist before working, so their clothes wouldn't get in the way and they were ready to serve. The word Peter uses for “clothe yourselves” paints exactly this picture: tying on a servant's apron. Humility is not a posture we strike now and then, but work clothes we put on every day. Perhaps Peter remembered the night the Lord “took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist” and knelt to wash his feet.

Verse 5 is addressed to “all of you”: the younger submit to the elder, and everyone submits to one another. The reason: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” In verse 6, “humble yourselves” means actively placing ourselves under God's mighty hand; in verse 7, “casting all your worries on him” is trust shown in action. The proud carry everything themselves; the humble hand their worries to the God who cares for them.

Humility faces two directions. Toward God, it means placing ourselves under his mighty hand and casting our worries on him; toward others, it means submitting to one another and gladly serving. The two are closely linked: those who will not hand their worries to God often try to control people. Here is the change of mindset: humility is not thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less, and of God and others more.
lessons.light: 321 Light: “God resists the proud” — pride puts us in a position of opposition to God. “He gives grace to the humble” — humility is the channel through which grace flows in, which is why humility is the key to revival. When I lay down power, return to my place, cast my worries on God and let God be God, I am set free.
q: Who is God? — “He cares for you.” How does this God regard your worries?
Who am I? — Is your humility more like a one-time posture or something you put on daily?
How shall I respond? — Whom will you “tie on the apron” to serve today, and what worry will you cast onto God?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist” and knelt to wash his disciples' feet (John 13:4–5). He was Lord, yet he put on a servant's work clothes. Peter protested at the time, but later he wrote, “clothe yourselves with humility” — he finally understood that the towel was meant for every follower.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you once wrapped a towel around your waist and washed my feet. Today I too want to clothe myself with humility and place myself under God's mighty hand. I cast the worries of my heart on you, because you care for me. Make me glad to submit and glad to serve, and let me receive the grace you give to the humble. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: As you dress in the morning, pray silently: “Lord, today I clothe myself with humility.”
Take on a serving task that someone else usually does
lessons.noon: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” — Lord, right now I clothe myself with humility.

lessons.title: Humility Meets Humility
lessons.theme: Only when we answer pride with humility can relationships become a win for both sides

v: Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits.
A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

lessons.still: Recall a person or situation that recently made you want to “hit back.” Don't think yet about what to say; just tell the Lord quietly, “Lord, let me be humble first.” Take three deep breaths, and with each one lay down a little more of the urge to win.
teach: When two people meet in a narrow alley, if both push forward with chests out, they collide; if one turns sideways to make room, the other usually turns sideways too. Pride stirs up pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. This is a principle we learned in the first stage; today we carry it into our most real conflicts.

Romans 12:16 has two “don'ts” and one “but”: don't set your mind on high things, don't be wise in your own conceits, but associate with the humble — all of them deal with the posture of putting ourselves above others in relationships. Proverbs 15:1 shows the chain reaction of words: a gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. A single sentence can start a fire, or put one out.

Humility meeting humility does not mean waiting for the other person to be humble first; it means I go first. When someone treats me with pride, if I respond with pride, it becomes self-rule against self-rule; if I respond with humility, I open the door for the Holy Spirit to work. This week we have seen the root, the faces and the remedy of pride; next week we face temptation — and pride is the very breach temptation most often exploits.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility draws out humility, and both sides win. This is also how God's kingdom system is built: not by anyone beating anyone else, but by stooping low for one another and building one another up. In 920, every “2” is someone with whom I practise the “0” of the self-emptied life, bearing the fruit of gentleness, patience and peace.
q: Who is God? — How does the God who associates with the humble treat you in your lowliness?
Who am I? — When faced with someone else's pride, how do you most often “hit back”?
How shall I respond? — With which of your “2” will you lead with a gentle answer today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus, “when he was cursed, didn't curse back. When he suffered, didn't threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). His gentleness was not weakness but a greater strength, which in the end overcame human pride and the schemes of Satan.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, when you were cursed you did not curse back, but entrusted yourself to the Father who judges righteously. In conflict, keep me from answering pride with pride; help me to be humble first and gentle first. Teach me to associate with the humble and not be wise in my own eyes. May my humility draw out humility in others, so that you receive the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: In a conversation that could become an argument, lower your voice and slow your speech first
Say to one of your “2”: “I was partly in the wrong in this too.”
Share with a spiritual companion one kind of pride you recognised in yourself this week
lessons.noon: “A gentle answer turns away wrath.” — Lord, right now let me be humble first.
